content: The effectiveness of alternative rabies diagnostic tests should be validated through multicenter studies conducted by WHO collaborating centers, national regulatory authorities, and control laboratories, in collaboration with manufacturers. The international standard for rabies vaccines is used to standardize the mouse protection test and in vitro assays for determining the glycoprotein (G protein) content. In 2008, a candidate vaccine was calibrated against the fifth international standard in a collaborative study and subsequently became the sixth international standard for rabies vaccines, with a potency of 8 IU/mL when reconstituted in 1 mL of distilled water. More than a dozen species or genotypes of lyssaviruses have been identified as causative agents of rabies, with RABV being the most common virus responsible for human rabies and the only virus used in current vaccines. However, existing vaccines may not provide protection against lyssaviruses outside of phylogroup I. Vaccine virus strains should be carefully selected, and their antigenic identity, as well as the identity and purity of the cell lines used for production, should be periodically evaluated. Comprehensive genetic characterization of vaccine virus strains through full genome sequencing is recommended. WHO has published general principles for the nonclinical and clinical evaluation of inactivated rabies vaccines. Preclinical testing, including immunogenicity studies and safety testing in animals, is a prerequisite for initiating human clinical trials. Clinical trials must adhere to WHO guidelines for good clinical practice and vaccine clinical trial design, conduct, and analysis, and must be approved by relevant national regulatory authorities. Currently, rabies vaccines are produced as individual doses for intramuscular injection, with a standard dose of 0.5 IU per dose suitable for both PrEP and PEP. However, the high cost of cell culture-based vaccines limits their widespread use in rabies-endemic areas. WHO promotes the intradermal administration of these vaccines as a safe, immunogenic, and cost-effective alternative to intramuscular administration, reducing vaccine volume and direct costs by 60–80%. Intradermal vaccination provides an equivalent immune response at a lower dose, making it a vaccine-sparing strategy for both PrEP and PEP. Both intradermal and intramuscular routes induce rapid recall immune responses upon booster immunization. Opened vaccine vials should be stored at 2–8°C for no longer than 6–8 hours. Scheduling follow-up PrEP visits for patients within similar timeframes can help minimize vaccine wastage. Intradermal administration remains cost-effective in all cases for both PrEP and PEP. Vaccine manufacturers should provide clinical evidence demonstrating that new products are immunogenic, effective, and safe when administered intradermally, and this suitability should be included on the product label. Administration should comply with WHO guidance and national health authority standards. Vaccines should be compared with those of known immunogenicity, efficacy, and safety, and serological testing using a fluorescent antibody virus neutralization (FAVN) test should be conducted, with results published in peer-reviewed journals. In countries where intradermal administration is approved for PrEP or PEP, manufacturers of vaccines proven safe and effective via this route should register their products for intradermal use and include this information in the product insert. Countries are encouraged to make regulatory amendments to allow cost-saving intradermal administration of rabies vaccines. Adverse events following active immunization with cell culture-based rabies vaccines (CCEEVs) are generally mild and well-tolerated. Minor, transient erythema, pain, or swelling at the injection site occurs in 35–45% of vaccinated individuals, particularly after intradermal administration of a booster dose. Mild systemic adverse events, such as transient fever, headache, dizziness, and gastrointestinal symptoms, are observed in 5–15% of cases. Serious adverse events, such as Guillain-Barré syndrome and allergic reactions, are rare. True vaccine failures are extremely rare when high-quality CCEEVs are used alongside proper wound care, adherence to the cold chain, and compliance with vaccination schedules. However, deviations from WHO-recommended protocols, such as failure to inject all bite sites or improper wound care, may contribute to treatment failure and subsequent death. CCEEVs establish immunological memory that is assumed to persist for life, even after neutralizing antibody titers decrease or become undetectable. Clinical data confirm that vaccinated individuals respond to booster immunization within seven days, even if the initial PrEP or PEP course was administered decades earlier. Failures of PEP, where patients die despite receiving the correct protocol in a timely manner, are extremely rare among the estimated 20 million people who receive PEP annually. Reported failures have occurred in developing countries and often involved deviations from WHO-recommended protocols, such as failure to inject all bite sites, lack of proper wound care, or use of poor-quality vaccines. Passive immunization with rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) is critical for patients with open wounds from suspected or confirmed rabid animals. Three classes of biological products are available for passive immunization: human rabies immunoglobulin (HRIG), equine rabies immunoglobulin (ERIG), and highly purified F(ab')2 fragments from equine immunoglobulin. RIG should be administered with the first dose of vaccine into and around the wound site. Thorough wound cleaning and irrigation, application of a potent antiseptic agent, and timely administration of the first CCEEV dose are key factors in increasing survival when RIG is unavailable. HRIG should be given at a maximum dose of 20 IU/kg of body weight, and ERIG at 40 IU/kg. ERIG is less expensive than HRIG, and newer equine preparations are potent, highly purified, and safe, with few adverse events. Serum sickness occurs in less than 1–3% of recipients, and the risk of anaphylactic reaction is low (1 in 150,000), with reactions generally treatable. Skin tests are not recommended before ERIG administration, as they poorly predict severe adverse events and should not prevent administration if needed. ERIG should be administered under conditions that allow management of an anaphylactic reaction. RIGs are in short supply globally, and monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) are being explored as alternatives. WHO has recommended mAb cocktails containing at least two antibodies against RABV for PEP. Several human mAbs have been tested, and the first single mAb was recently licensed by the Serum Institute of India, showing equivalent performance to HRIG. Recombinant technology used in mAb production reduces issues related to availability, safety, and purity. mAbs should be recommended for public health programs based on epidemiological and geographical settings, with monitoring of safety and efficacy during post-marketing use.
